articles.title: 11 dead in Manipur over spurious liquor consumption, over 300 hospitalised
articles.summary: Imphal: At least 11 people have died since November 18 in incidents linked to consumption of spurious alcohol in Manipur's Chandel district, while more than 300 others have been hospitalised. The patients are mostly from Chakpikarong and surrounding areas and have been hospitalised across multiple healthcare facilities in Imphal, including JNIMS, RIMS, Shija and Babina Hospital. Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh visited Shija Hospital and Babina Hospital on Friday afternoon to assess the situation and meet patients undergoing treatment. In a social media post, Singh said, "Visited Shija Hospital at Lamphelpat, and Babina Hospital at Sajiwa, today (on Friday) to enquire about the health condition of the persons undergoing treatment after consuming spurious liquor from Chakpikarong area in Chandel District." 8 die in three days after 'consuming spurious liquor' in Manipur "Over 140 patients were admitted to Shija Hospital and over 41 patients at Babina Hospital. The death toll has touched 11 during the last 48 hours. The patients are undergoing medical evaluation and treatment under the close supervision of the doctors," he said. "A medical team, led by a Specialist in General Medicine, along with essential medicines, has left for Chandel District to strengthen on-ground treatment and response", he said adding, "The government will conduct an enquiry and the culprits will be punished." Joint Managing Director of Shija Hospitals, Chetan K, told reporters that the patients admitted to the hospital reported symptoms of dizziness, stomach pain and other complications. "Some patients are also undergoing hemodialysis", he added. A JNIMS doctor said, "Many of the hospitalised include individuals who had consumed local liquor and had come to the hospital due to fear." Shija Hospitals also informed that "over 312 patients (have been) attended (to) till now at Shija Hospitals due to Methanol poisoning." Preliminary reports suggest that the suspected contaminated alcohol was purchased from Sugnu in Kakching district. Chandel constituency MLA SS Olish said arrangements are being made to bring more patients up to Imphal and has requested the chief minister to look into the situation. She said, "I have spoken personally to CM Yumnam Khemchand, and requested him to look into the situation affecting Chandel. articles.title: No change in position on Indus Waters Treaty: India as Pakistan Minister attends SCO forum in Delhi
articles.summary: The Ministry of External Affairs on Friday said that India's position on the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) is "very clear" and there has been "absolutely no change" in it while Pakistan Minister Musadik Malik is in Delhi to attend the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum. Malik attended the opening day of the three-day forum on Friday. The event, being hosted by India at the historic Purana Quila, was inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. India had announced on October 28 that invitations had been extended to all SCO members, including Pakistan, in keeping with established practice. Culture has key role in fostering dialogue: Pakistan minister Musadik Malik at SCO forum in Delhi It was the first time a Pakistani minister was invited to an even since the May 7-10 military hostilities last year following Operation Sindoor. Pakistan had announced on November 14 that its Climate Change Minister Malik would participate in the forum. Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal, at a press briefing, was asked how New Delhi viewed Malik's participation in the India-hosted forum, given that he does not hold the culture portfolio and had reportedly made comments on the IWT. "As far as IWT is concerned, we have made our position very clear, and that is where it remains. There is absolutely no change," Jaiswal said. India kept the IWT in abeyance in 2025 as a measure against Pakistan following the April 22 Pahalgam terror attack that claimed the lives of 26 people. Experts view Malik's participation as an opportunity in a multilateral framework that may help improve ties between the two neighbours. Interacting with the media at the forum, Malik said culture has a key role in fostering better relations between India and Pakistan. Hours before the inauguration, the MEA said the forum was a "multilateral event within the SCO framework", for which invitations had been extended to all members of the grouping, including Pakistan. "India is hosting the 1st SCO Civilisation Dialogue on 20-22 November 2026, in New Delhi. This is a multilateral event within the SCO framework, for which invitations have been extended to all members of the SCO, including Pakistan," the MEA said in a post on X. "Observers and Dialogue Partners of the SCO have also been invited to attend the Dialogue, which will be inaugurated this evening by the Hon’ble Prime Minister," it said. The event is being hosted by the Ministry of Culture and the MEA. The SCO was founded at a summit in Shanghai in 2001 by the presidents of Russia, China, the Kyrgyz Republic, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. India and Pakistan became its permanent members in 2017. (With PTI inputs)

articles.summary: New Delhi: A day after the UN's top court ruled that Myanmar "committed genocide" against the Rohingya group in 2017, India on Friday said it has "taken note of the verdict" and asserted that New Delhi "consistently supported" the safe, speedy and sustainable return of the displaced Rohingya people from Rakhine state. At his bi-weekly media briefing, Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal was asked to comment on the historic judgment by the International Court of Justice (ICJ). "On the ICJ verdict… we have taken note of the verdict. India has consistently supported safe, speedy and sustainable return of the displaced Rohingya people from the Rakhine state," Jaiswal said. "To this end, India had earlier, as you would be aware, supported Rohingya camps in Bangladesh with relief supplies in five tranches under Operation Insaniyat. We have also supported the Rakhine State Development Programme in Myanmar for this purpose," he added. Important step forward for international justice, return of Rohingya: Sheikh Hasina on ICJ ruling The International Court of Justice on Thursday ruled that Myanmar "committed genocide" against the Rohingya in the northern Rakhine state during the 2017 "clearance operations", in violation of its obligations under the Genocide Convention. The top UN court also ordered the Southeast Asian nation to allow the tens of thousands of people who fled the violence to return home. The case against Myanmar concerning alleged violations of the Genocide Convention was brought by The Gambia in November, 2019. ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said the court, in a 9-6 decision, found that Myanmar "has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine state, in violation of its obligations under the Genocide Convention". Bangladesh, which hosts over one million Rohingya refugees, welcomed the judgment, describing it as a significant development for justice and resolving the protracted refugee crisis. Most of the Rohingya refugees fled Myanmar's Rakhine state to evade persecution after a 2017 army crackdown in their homeland. Jaiswal was also asked how India viewed the recent meeting of the leaders from Russia, China, and the US, who sat for a trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China. "So, we have taken note of this meeting between the three APEC member countries. We await a fuller accounting of the concrete outcomes of the meeting before offering our assessment. So, that is what we have to say," he said. Another query was related to the recent Quad Summit held in Manila. The summit seemed to have been hosted by the US in Manila. Does this mean that India has now "relinquished its chairmanship, presidency of the Quad", and that there will not be a Quad Summit in India in the near future, or does India still hope to host a Quad Summit over here, a reporter asked. "We had the Quad Summit in Manila, and the four leaders of the Quad member countries met. We issued a statement, which you would have seen. There were some concrete outcomes which came out of it, including a Quad Business Leaders Forum, which is to be held next year, I think. "Also on emerging technologies, AI, maritime surveillance, on cable connectivity in the region, on several of these issues, including cybersecurity cooperation, and on security matters. So, the statement of the leaders is very clear that all these items, these decisions are practical cooperation, delivering good for people and countries in the Indo-Pacific region. In so far as the question of chairmanship is concerned, let me come back to you with details on that," he added. Jaiswal, when asked about some statements coming out of the US Commission of International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) levelling allegations against the Indian government in connection with voter rolls, said, "On USCIRF, I want to repeat what I have said earlier that we see it as a biased organisation with a blatantly political agenda, and I don't think an organisation which is so prejudiced needs to be taken seriously."

articles.title: Bowl me over! Five wholesome, easy-to-make bowl meals to warm up your winter
articles.summary: Winter is here, and appetites tend to grow with the chill. With a few wholesome ingredients and a little imagination, you can bring flavours from around the world to your table. There’s something comforting about a meal served in a bowl. Here are five easy-to-make recipes, each scaled for a generous serving, and customisable. Buddha Bowl A Buddha Bowl combines whole grains, vegetables, plant-based protein, and a delicious dressing. There is no fixed recipe, which makes it perfect for experimenting. The idea is to create a meal that is as nourishing as it is visually appealing. Ingredients (one bowl) — ½ cup cooked quinoa or brown rice — ¼ cup boiled chickpeas — ¼ cup roasted sweet potato cubes — ¼ cup cucumber/red radish, chopped or sliced — ¼ cup grated carrot — ¼ avocado, sliced — A handful of spinach or lettuce — Salt and pepper to taste For the dressing — 1 tbsp tahini or peanut butter — 1 tsp lemon juice — 1 tsp olive oil — 1 tsp honey — 1-2 tbsp water — A pinch of salt Method Take the cooked quinoa, chickpeas, roasted sweet potato, and fresh vegetables in a bowl. Whisk together the dressing ingredients until smooth and drizzle generously over the bowl. Finish with sesame seeds or pumpkin seeds to add some crunch. Replace quinoa with millets, chickpeas with paneer or tofu, and add seasonal vegetables for an Indian twist. Buddha Bowl Lebanese-inspired falafel bowl Lebanese food can be a real protein jackpot. Fresh greens, juicy tomatoes, cucumber, olives, and ruby-red pomegranate seeds add colour, crunch, and a burst of freshness. It is a complete meal that is both filling and refreshing. Ingredients (one bowl) — 2 small falafel balls — 3 tbsp hummus — ¼ cup boiled chickpeas — ¼ cup cucumber, diced — ¼ cup tomatoes, diced — ¼ cup shredded lettuce — 2 tbsp grated carrot — 4-5 black or green olives, sliced — 1 tbsp pomegranate seeds — 1 tbsp chopped parsley or coriander — 2 tbsp pita bread pieces (optional) For the lemon-olive oil dressing — 1 tbsp olive oil — 1 tsp lemon juice — ¼ tsp roasted cumin powder — A pinch of black pepper and salt Method Spread the hummus generously at the base or along one side of a wide serving bowl. Arrange the boiled chickpeas, cucumber, tomatoes, lettuce, and carrots around it. Place the warm falafel balls in the centre. Add olives and pomegranate seeds for a burst of colour. Whisk together the dressing ingredients and drizzle over the salad. Garnish with parsley or coriander and serve with toasted pita bread. Lebanese-inspired falafel bowl Donburi It’s a traditional Japanese dish in which rice is topped with vegetables or tofu. Ingredients (one bowl) — ¾ cup cooked sushi rice or regular short-grain rice — ½ cup firm tofu, cubed — ¼ avocado, sliced — ¼ cup cucumber, diced — ¼ cup ripe mango, diced — 2 tbsp boiled edamame or green peas — 1 tbsp shredded cabbage — 1 tsp sesame seeds — A little nori (seaweed), shredded For the dressing — 1 tbsp soy sauce — 1 tsp rice vinegar or lemon juice — ½ tsp honey — ½ tsp sesame oil — A pinch of chilli flakes Method Pan-fry the tofu cubes until lightly golden. Place the cooked rice in a bowl and arrange the tofu, avocado, cucumber, mango, edamame, and cabbage over it. Mix the dressing ingredients and drizzle over the bowl. Garnish with sesame seeds and shredded seaweed. For a warmer, more traditional Donburi-inspired version, simmer the tofu and vegetables briefly in soy sauce, ginger, and a little stock before spooning them over hot rice. Donburi Bibimbap Bibimbap literally means 'mixed rice' in Korean, and it is a wonderful example of how simple ingredients can create a memorable meal. Traditionally served with rice and sautéed vegetables, the dish is arranged beautifully before being mixed together just before eating. Ingredients (one bowl) — ¾ cup cooked rice (short-grain rice) — ¼ cup grated carrot — ¼ cup sliced mushrooms — ¼ cup spinach — ¼ cup bean sprouts — ¼ cucumber, cut into thin strips — 1 tsp sesame oil — 1 tsp sesame seeds — Salt to taste For the sauce — 1 tbsp gochujang (Korean chilli paste) — 1 tsp soy sauce — 1 tsp honey — 1 tsp sesame oil — 1 tsp water Method Lightly sauté the carrots, mushrooms, spinach, and bean sprouts separately with a little sesame oil and salt. Arrange the warm rice at the bottom of a bowl, and place each vegetable in separate sections on top. Mix the sauce ingredients and drizzle over the bowl. Sprinkle with sesame seeds. Mix everything together before eating. No gochujang? A mixture of chilli paste, soy sauce, and a little honey makes a convenient substitute. The contrasting colours and textures are what make this bowl so inviting. Bibimbap Khow Suey If comfort food had an international ambassador, Khow Suey would be a strong contender. Originating in Burma (Myanmar), this popular noodle dish features noodles submerged in a fragrant coconut milk curry and topped with an assortment of crunchy, tangy, and spicy accompaniments. Ingredients (one bowl) — 1 cup cooked noodles — ½ cup coconut milk — ¼ cup vegetable stock or water — ¼ cup mixed vegetables (carrot, beans and capsicum) — 1 tbsp finely chopped onion — 1 tsp ginger-garlic paste — ½ tsp curry powder — ¼ tsp turmeric — 1 tsp oil — Salt to taste For the toppings — 1 tbsp sliced fried onions — 1 tsp roasted peanuts — 1 tsp chopped coriander — 1 tsp lemon juice — A little chilli oil — A few crispy noodles Method Heat oil in a pan and sauté the onion and ginger-garlic paste. Add curry powder, turmeric, and vegetables. Cook for two minutes. Pour in coconut milk and stock, season with salt, and simmer for 5–7 minutes until the curry thickens slightly. Place cooked noodles in a bowl and pour the hot coconut curry over them. Finish with fried onions, peanuts, coriander, lemon juice, and crispy noodles. Keeping the winter chill out: Simple, inexpensive ways to make your home warmer
articles.summary: When temperatures dip, keeping your home warm and comfortable becomes a priority. You don’t need expensive heating systems or major renovations to keep the chill at bay. From making the most of natural sunlight to repurposing everyday household items, a few practical changes can make a difference. Here are some expert-backed tips to create a cosier home this season. Make the most of your home Natural sunlight is one of the easiest ways to warm up a home. Mark D’Souza, a Chennai-based interior designer, suggests keeping windows and curtains open during the day, “particularly in rooms that receive direct sunlight”. Allow the sun to warm floors and walls. As evening approaches, draw the curtains to minimise heat loss, he adds. Cold air often enters through gaps beneath doors and around window frames. Shivani Singhania, a Mysuru-based architect, recommends placing rolled-up towels or old blankets along the bottom of doors to minimise draughts. For a more lasting solution, consider inexpensive adhesive weather-stripping. Rearranging furniture can also make a difference. “Avoid placing frequently used seating directly beside draughty windows, balcony doors, or exterior entrances. Instead, move chairs towards areas that receive afternoon sunlight,” she adds. Keep balcony doors closed during chilly evenings, particularly on windy days, and seal any noticeable gaps. Let natural sunlight stream in during the day to warm up your home. Pay attention to damp corners too. “Moisture on walls and around windows can make rooms feel uncomfortable,” says Shivani. Check behind furniture and inside cupboards for signs of dampness, and address leaks and condensation promptly. Repurpose what you have Bring out quilts, blankets, and throws that have been tucked away in cupboards. “Layering blankets on beds helps retain body heat, while keeping a few along with multiple cushions on the sofa makes chilly evenings more comfortable,” explains Mark. Cotton flannel, fleece, and woollen fabrics are particularly useful for adding warmth. Cold tiled and stone floors can make mornings uncomfortable. “Place existing dhurries, rugs, or thick cotton mats in frequently used areas, such as beside the bed or near the sofa. Even a small layer can make a difference to how the floor feels underfoot,” says Mark. Experts suggest temporary fabric coverings for a home with large windows, as “they can provide an additional barrier during particularly chilly hours”. Ensure these are securely fitted and do not obstruct ventilation or create a fire hazard. Remove them during the day to let sunlight in. Small everyday adjustments Getting into a cold bed can be unpleasant. A hot-water bag can provide warmth on chilly nights. “Fill it with hot water, secure the stopper and use a protective cover. Place it under the blanket or between the sheets for 10-15 minutes before bedtime and remove it before getting in,” shares Shivani. You could also add an extra blanket to retain body heat. Lighting can also influence how warm a room feels. Mark suggests replacing harsh, cool-white bulbs with warm-white LED alternatives. “Though they do not significantly raise indoor temperatures, table lamps and decorative lights can create a softer, cosier ambience,” Mark adds. While keeping windows shut helps retain warmth, ventilation remains essential. Open them during the warmer part of the day to allow fresh air to circulate, particularly in kitchens and bathrooms where moisture accumulates. Close them as temperatures drop. If certain rooms are rarely used, keep their doors closed to concentrate everyday activities in frequently occupied spaces, without compromising ventilation or safety, Mark suggests.

‘I want to be a part of cinema till I die’: Rajisha Vijayan on her acting journey
articles.summary: From her compelling performances in Malayalam cinema to carving a niche for herself across South Indian film industries, Rajisha Vijayan has steadily established herself as an actor who isn't afraid to experiment with roles. Known for bringing authenticity, depth, and nuance to her characters, she has consistently chosen stories that challenge her as a performer. With her latest outing, 'Bachelor Party 2', Rajisha adds another interesting project to her filmography. In this conversation with Ikyatha Yerasala , she opens up about her journey as an actor, her upbringing across various cities in India, and more. How have your expectations from a script evolved over the years? I look for something that sparks my interest and makes me feel excited about taking it on. I look for something that I haven't explored before. When I hear a script, I should feel that this is a story that needs to be told and that I want to be a part of it. I'd also love to portray more well-written female characters. Do women actors have the same freedom and opportunities as their male counterparts to experiment with roles and reinvent themselves? Honestly, it depends on the project. A film is ultimately a director's vision, and we are all just tools that a director uses to tell the story. Some directors are very particular and have clarity about what they want, while others are more open to improvisation, suggestions, and collaboration. That said, the industry and its market are largely male-driven. Cinema may be an art form, but at the end of the day, it is also a business. An actor has to be commercially viable and be able to draw money in. There are very few films where even if a male actor is shouldering the film, the female character is given an equally substantial role rather than being treated as an accessory. It isn't just about the roles you choose; the director and the script have to choose you, too. Rajisha Vijayan. More than a decade after your award-winning debut, how has your understanding of success evolved? Success, to me right now, is to stay sustainable. Initially, it was about whether I could become an actor, and it later became about making a mark and getting projects. After a few years, it becomes about not getting washed away by the current and standing your ground, doing good work, creating a brand in your name and making people think about the characters you have played. I want to be a part of cinema till the day I die. Has there been a role that changed the way you look at the world? My Tamil debut, 'Karnan', was one such experience. I grew up across different parts of the country as an Army child. In the defence community, everyone is treated equally, without discrimination or divisions. So, I had very little exposure to caste-based discrimination. While shooting for 'Karnan', I was shaken by the realisation that caste divisions continue to exist even today. Learning about the atrocities faced by communities because of caste was really shocking for me. Another such role was in the movie 'Mastishka Maranam'. Many of the issues explored in the film are relevant even today, and being part of it gave me a different perspective on several things. Growing up in an Army family meant living in different parts of the country. How did these experiences shape your outlook on life? I've lived in places such as Pune, Agartala and Punjab, among others. Travelling and meeting people from different backgrounds really broaden your horizons and opens up your way of thinking. You experience cultural differences and sometimes even cultural shocks. Things that might be considered inappropriate in one part of the country could be perfectly acceptable in another. It also makes you more adaptable. I believe people everywhere have a lot of love to give; they just express it differently. In Punjab, people are more extroverted and shower you with affection. In Bengal, too, there is plenty of warmth, but it is expressed more subtly. Women in Bengal stand out because they are powerhouses. In Kerala, I've found people to be quite open to different ideas. These experiences have taught me to appreciate how beautifully diverse our country is. And then there's the food! As Indians, we are truly blessed to have such an incredible variety of cuisines. Naga and other Northeastern cuisines are also absolutely delicious. If you could choose your next role without worrying about commercial success or audience expectations, what kind of character would you like to explore? I'd love to do a rom-com because I feel we're really lacking in that genre today. The more positive spectrum of human emotions is not being explored enough on screen. We're seeing a lot of action, horror and violence, and I really miss chick flicks, romantic comedies and those gut-wrenching love stories. I would also love to do an out-and-out comedy or a spoof film that families can watch together and laugh their hearts out. Are you open to doing a Kannada film in the future? Of course! I've already explored three South Indian languages, and I would like to explore Kannada projects. Whenever I visit Bengaluru, many people recognise me through 'June', my Malayalam film. I admire Kannada actors such as Rishab Shetty and Rakshit Shetty, and I think Kannada is a culturally rich language. I loved films such as 'Sapta Saagaradaache Ello' and 'Gantumoote'. I'd also love to explore Hindi cinema, as it's a language I speak fluently.

articles.title: The sun doesn't know it's winter: Why sunscreen is essential year-round
articles.summary: It’s common to hear, “Doctor, I stopped using sunscreen because there isn’t much sunlight”, during the winter months. Cooler weather makes sunlight feel less intense, but your skin does not interpret sunshine quite the way you do. The sun does not take a holiday UVB contributes to sunburn, while UVA contributes to pigmentation and premature ageing. Seasonal UV levels vary, but UVA remains relevant throughout the year and can pass through ordinary window glass. Melanin provides some natural protection, but it does not make your skin immune to sun damage. Melasma, uneven skin tone, and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation can persist throughout the year. Visible light can also worsen pigmentation in susceptible individuals. Choosing sunscreen Select a broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher. In winter, a moisturising formula may be more comfortable. People with melasma may benefit from tinted sunscreen containing iron oxides. How much is enough? Apply a generous, even layer to exposed skin, including the ears, neck, and hands. Reapply every two hours during prolonged outdoor exposure and after swimming or heavy sweating. Indoor needs depend on sunlight exposure, especially when sitting near windows. If I use SPF50+ sunscreen every day do I need to take vitamin D? Can moisturiser replace sunscreen? Only if it is specifically labelled as offering adequate SPF and broad-spectrum protection. Otherwise, moisturiser and sunscreen serve different purposes. A moisturising sunscreen can conveniently provide both. Sunscreen is preventive healthcare, not merely a cosmetic step. It helps reduce photoageing, pigmentation problems, and the risk of skin cancer. Enjoy the winter sunshine, but remember — cooler temperatures do not necessarily mean less ultraviolet exposure. (The author is a consultant dermatologist)

articles.title: Curious case of India’s fugitive tycoons: Wanted at home, welcome abroad
articles.summary: In November 2005, Portugal put Abu Salem on a plane to Mumbai. Lisbon had few doubts. India wanted him for the 1993 Bombay blasts, which killed more than 250 people. Portugal sought only two guarantees: that he would not be hanged and that he would not serve more than 25 years. India gave its word. In 2022, the Supreme Court held the government to that promise. From arrest to handover took three years. By the standards of extradition, that is almost brisk. Twelve years later, in June 2017, Vijay Mallya sat in the stands at The Oval in London and watched India play cricket. He had left the year before, owing the banks around Rs 9,000 crore. India’s formal request for his extradition had been made four months earlier. He lost his appeals in the English courts by 2020. He is still in England. Nine cricket seasons have come and gone. Why does the bomber return home in three years, while the businessman can still enjoy cricket in England? These two scenes explain the numbers better than any white paper. Between 2019 and July 2026, India brought back 274 fugitives from 36 countries. Only nine faced fraud or financial charges. The remaining fugitives were wanted on charges such as murder, sexual offences, organised crime, terrorism and drug trafficking. Is the easy reading – that our diplomats and law-enforcement agencies fail when the man is rich – really the better one? Or does the world simply agree on some crimes and not on others? Murder is murder in Lisbon and in Lucknow. A bomb in a crowded market horrifies every jurisdiction. No country wants a killer living down the street. When India asks for one, the host state is usually relieved to see him go. It will demand assurances on the death penalty and prison conditions, then hand him over. A financial crime carries no such moral weight. It exists because a statute says it does. Extradition treaties reflect this through dual criminality: the alleged conduct itself must be an offence in both countries. Courts look past the label and ask whether the same acts would be criminal under their own law. A wilful default, a breach of foreign-exchange rules, or a money-laundering charge resting on an Indian predicate offence may find no counterpart abroad. What Delhi calls fraud, London may call a failed business. Nirav Modi’s counsel described the PNB affair as “ill-advised lending”. Mallya’s team said Kingfisher was an airline that went bust, as airlines do. Is a balance-sheet failure the same offence as a bomb in a market? Most foreign courts answer no. The big cases cleared that first hurdle. English magistrates found a case for Mallya and Nirav Modi to answer. Belgian judges accepted six of the seven charges against Mehul Choksi. But clearing dual criminality only opens the next gates. The foreign court asks whether the prison is safe and whether the trial will be fair. It also examines whether the prosecution has political motives. A person accused of violent crimes loses sympathy at each gate. A non-violent one does not. He arrives in a suit, with a medical file and the best barristers money can buy. In February 2025, the English High Court refused to send the arms dealer Sanjay Bhandari to India. It feared for his safety in Tihar. Every lawyer in London trying to shield a fugitive from extradition has read that judgment. How many more such judgments must we collect before we notice the pattern? Now consider how the host country sees him. For years Britain sold residence to the wealthy through its investor visa. It closed that scheme only in 2022. Antigua sold Choksi its citizenship in 2017. Belgium hosted him as a resident whose wife is a Belgian national. Lalit Modi has acquired a British passport. One country’s economic offender becomes another country’s entrepreneur, or refugee, or its favoured guest. A man who brings capital is welcome. A man who brings a gun is not. Is that hypocrisy peculiar to the West? Or is it simply how states have always behaved? Our own politics make the problem worse. When ministers and rival parties turn a fugitive into a campaign slogan, they hand his lawyers a gift. Political persecution is a defence in every extradition treaty. The louder the speeches in Delhi, the stronger the affidavit in London. Does a fugitive gain more from Indian TV channels than from any loophole in the law? SANJAY HEGDE India should also look in the mirror. Sheikh Hasina has lived in Delhi since August 2024. A Bangladeshi tribunal sentenced her to death in absentia last November. Dhaka wants her back. New Delhi has not sent her, citing treaty safeguards, as other countries do when dealing with India. To Dhaka, she is a convict. To Delhi, she is a guest whose life may be in danger. This is not to make a judgment on her case but to underscore that the principle of sovereign discretion cuts both ways. If every sovereign keeps the right to decide whom it shelters, why should the same right not be exercised against India? What, then, should India do? First, accept that the world will never treat a defaulter like a terrorist. Will shouting change that? Second, fix what foreign judges examine. They read reports on our prisons. They count the years our undertrials wait. A country where trials drag on for a decade gives every fugitive his best argument. Our assurances work only if our courts can enforce them. The Abu Salem judgment showed that they can. Third, follow the money rather than the man. The Fugitive Economic Offenders Act lets India confiscate assets. The government says it has recovered over Rs 14,000 crore from Mallya’s assets alone. For the banks, is recovering the money more important than bringing him back to face justice? Diplomacy has its place. Foreign secretaries can press their counterparts, and prime ministers can raise names at summits. But extradition is a legal process conducted in foreign courts, under foreign law, by judges who owe us nothing. They will send back the bomber without much fuss. They will think long and hard about the businessman. Abu Salem sits in Taloja jail. Mallya watches cricket in England. Does this reflect a failure of nerve in South Block, or simply how the world ranks crimes? India can grumble about that ranking, or it can make its courts and prisons a place a foreign judge would trust. (The writer is a senior advocate designated by the Supreme Court)

articles.title: Pannun murder conspiracy case: US court sentences Indian national Nikhil Gupta to 235 months in jail
articles.summary: A US federal judge on Friday sentenced Indian national Nikhil Gupta to 235 months in jail for his involvement in a murder-for-hire plot against Khalistani separatist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York. US District Judge Victor Marrero in the Southern District of New York announced the verdict. Indian national Nikhil Gupta to be sentenced on Friday in murder-for-hire plot Gupta, 55, had pleaded guilty earlier this year to charges of murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering, in connection with his efforts to murder Pannun. Pannun, who holds dual American and Canadian citizenship, was present in the court when the verdict was announced. In a 20-page submission to Judge Marrero, United States Attorney James McDonald said Gupta's "conduct was as brutal as it was brazen. "He was a crucial participant in a foreign plot to execute a US citizen on US soil. The Court should impose a sentence that reflects the magnitude of the crime and sends a message that the violent silencing of voices in this country will not be tolerated. For these reasons, and all the reasons set forth above, the Government respectfully requests that the Court impose a sentence of 293 months' imprisonment," the US government said. They said that Gupta and his co-conspirators, "including at least one Indian Government employee", plotted to kill an American citizen on US soil because of the "victim's political ideology. Earlier, the same court had ordered the delivery of summonses to National Security Advisor Ajit Doval and former Research and Analysis Wing (RAW) chief Samant Goel through Delhi courts in connection with a lawsuit filed by Pannun. Pannun is wanted by Indian probe agencies on various terror charges. In an order dated November 13, the court directed its clerk to send the summonses and accompanying judicial documents to the Patiala House District Court for Doval, and the Dwarka and Tis Hazari district courts for Goel. "The court respectfully requests the assistance of receiving Indian courts in effecting service of process upon the defendants in this civil action pending before this court," says an order by Judge Katherine Polk Failla. Pannun murder conspiracy case: US court orders delivery of summonses to Ajit Doval, former RAW chief through Delhi courts Citing the Hague Conventions and relevant provisions of the Indian Code of Civil Procedure (CPC), Failla said foreign courts can serve summonses to Doval and Goel through Indian courts. The CPC permits summonses issued by foreign civil courts notified by the central government to be transmitted to Indian courts and served in the same manner as summonses issued by domestic courts. The US court order stated that the standard procedure for serving the summonses through India's central authority under the Hague Convention had been attempted but rejected. The court subsequently authorised an alternative mode of service under Article 19 of the convention and the relevant provisions of India's CPC. Pannun, a US-based legal counsel for the banned organisation Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), has filed the civil lawsuit seeking damages over an alleged attempt on his life. He has accused Doval of orchestrating the alleged assassination plot with the involvement of India's external intelligence agency RAW. Last month, the US court attempted to deliver the summonses to Doval and Goel through a diplomatic note issued by the State Department to the Indian Embassy in Washington India has rejected the lawsuit, calling it "fabricated and malicious". "We reject the fabricated and malicious attacks on our high officials. Also, we reject the frivolous lawsuits. A request for serving of judicial documents in India can only be routed through India's designated central authority, which is the Ministry of Law and Justice," External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said on November 10. The US government is not a party to this case. The civil lawsuit is separate from the US criminal proceedings against Gupta and former RAW officer Vikash Yadav.
